where: Section 2, Worked example 1, and Quiz Q3
problem: Every exponent has lost its superscript, so the formulas and the arithmetic read as wrong. "C = Me mod n", "M = Cd mod n", "gx mod p", "gxy mod p" look like products of variables named Me or Cd. In the worked example the lines "53 mod 33 = 125", "262 = 676", "264 ≡ 162 = 256", "267 = 264 × 262 × 26" are nonsense as printed; the quiz answer "C = 73 mod 55 = 343 mod 55 = 13" and "1327 mod 55" have the same problem. A student cannot follow the squaring steps or copy the formula correctly.
fix: Use superscript markup everywhere: C = M<sup>e</sup> mod n, M = C<sup>d</sup> mod n, g<sup>x</sup> mod p, g<sup>xy</sup> mod p. Worked example: C = 5<sup>3</sup> mod 33 = 125 mod 33 = 26. Decrypt: M = 26<sup>7</sup> mod 33; 26<sup>2</sup> = 676 ≡ 16; 26<sup>4</sup> ≡ 16<sup>2</sup> = 256 ≡ 25; 26<sup>7</sup> = 26<sup>4</sup> × 26<sup>2</sup> × 26 ≡ 25 × 16 × 26; 25 × 16 = 400 ≡ 4; 4 × 26 = 104 ≡ 5 mod 33. Quiz: C = 7<sup>3</sup> mod 55 = 343 mod 55 = 13, and decrypting 13<sup>27</sup> mod 55 returns 7.

problem: x and y appear in g<sup>x</sup> and g<sup>xy</sup> without ever being defined, so the reader cannot tell which values are secret and which are public. The phrase "with public prime p and base g" also leaves the impression that the exponents are public too.
fix: Say: each side picks a secret random exponent (x for one side, y for the other) and sends g<sup>x</sup> mod p and g<sup>y</sup> mod p over the open channel; p and g are public, x and y stay secret, and both sides compute the shared secret g<sup>xy</sup> mod p.

problem: It says only a stateless filter cannot inspect malware inside encrypted HTTPS on port 443. A stateful firewall cannot do that either, so the trap understates the limitation and contradicts Section 4, which says plainly that a firewall fails to see encrypted malware inside port 443.
fix: Write: no packet-filtering firewall, stateless or stateful, can inspect malware hidden inside encrypted HTTPS traffic on port 443; it can only allow or block the connection.

problem: The condition on e is incomplete: the chapter gives e·d ≡ 1 mod φ(n) but never states that e must be coprime with φ(n), which is exactly why the inverse d exists. A student may pick e = 2 and find no d.
fix: Add: e must satisfy gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1, which guarantees that d exists.
